headline: A requirement this toolkit already refuses at parse is not one a profile owes a rule.
summary: The Microsoft Trusted Root Program requirements ship as `microsoft-root`, named and never detected like the other two root programs. Two of the twenty clauses that looked certificate-observable turned out to be enforced already: a certificate that is not X.509 v3 and an end entity whose basicConstraints carries a pathLenConstraint are both refused before a rule sees them, so neither got a row and both got a vector proving the verdict an operator actually sees.

Added: `pki.lint.certificate(der, { profile: "microsoft-root" })` runs the Microsoft Trusted Root Program profile. Naming it is the only way to reach these rows, and passing no profile leaves every one of them inert.

Section 3.A.2 states the scope of the root rules outright, that a certificate added to the store is a self-signed root, so those rows read matching issuer and subject names together with the key identifiers. A CA reissued in its own name under a new key carries both names and was signed by its predecessor. The root rows read the key identifiers and pass over it, and the issuing CA rows read the names and pass over it too, because the bytes do not tell it from the succession certificate a root issues to its replacement. That is the reading `mozilla-root` and `chrome-root` already carry, so the three agree.

The section 3.A.1.4 keyUsage rules over a root: the extension is required, it must be critical, and `keyCertSign` and `cRLSign` must both be set, each missing bit naming itself. Its remaining sentence conditions `digitalSignature` on the root key signing OCSP responses, which is what the private key is used for rather than anything the certificate carries. Section 3.A.1.1 requires a commonName; that it identifies the publisher and is unique are not settled by one certificate.

The section 3.A.3 term of eight to 25 years, measured in months so a day-of-month with no counterpart clamps. The clause measures from the date of submission, which is at or after notBefore, so a term measured from notBefore is the longest the certificate can offer from any submission date: under eight years is under eight years from every one of them and is an error, while over 25 years from notBefore can still meet 25 years from a later submission and is a warning that says so.

The section 3.A.5 requirement that an issuing CA certificate carry a distribution point or an authorityInfoAccess naming an OCSP responder, and the section 3.A.8 separation of uses. Its sentence that no issuing CA may combine server authentication with S/MIME, code signing or time stamping is an error, naming the purpose found beside it. Its other two sentences are broader, asking that all four uses be separated and that a separate intermediate serve each, so a pair they forbid and that sentence does not is a warning.

The section 3.A.10 requirement that an end entity certificate declare one of the seventeen reserved policy identifiers the clause lists, all of which were already in the OID registry, and the section 3.A.14 rule that a certificate naming `id-kp-OCSPSigning` name no other extended key usage.

The section 3.B signature and key table: a signature algorithm outside the RSA and ECDSA forms of SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, an RSA modulus under 2048 bits, an elliptic curve outside NIST P-256, P-384 and P-521, and a key of a family the table does not name. For code signing and time stamping use, which a certificate declares through its own extended key usage, the table adds that elliptic curve keys are not supported, that an RSA modulus above 4096 bits is not, and that a root needs at least 4096.

The section 3.E.2 list of extended key usages the program enables on a root, reported as a warning naming the purpose. The document disagrees with itself here: that list omits `id-kp-codeSigning` while all of section 3.D governs code signing roots and states that all code signing certificates are treated equally. Reporting a code signing root would contradict that section, so the admitted set takes the reading that reports neither.
Changed: `pki.lint.rules()` enumerates the new rows, which stay inert under the default rule set because each one asks whether the caller named the profile.
Fixed: A CMC conformance vector for a `NoSignatureValue` that is not an OCTET STRING drew its value from a SHA-256 digest, and random bytes read as a complete OCTET STRING whenever the first two are `04 1E`, so about one run in 65536 the vector presented the very shape it asked the reader to refuse. It now uses an INTEGER, which is never an OCTET STRING. Nothing in the published tarball changes.
